text.p: America Online Inc., recently forced to offer refunds under pressure from angry customers and dozens of state attorneys general, Thursday reported a $155 million loss for its fiscal second quarter.
But there were two rays of sunshine for the world's largest online service.

The company -- surprised by a huge upsurge in subscribers and the time they spent online when it switched to flat-rate pricing in December -- said it would be able to serve all members by the end of April because it was leasing 50,000 more modems to expand its network capacity.
America Online, or AOL, also said it had seen substantial increases in revenues from advertising and electronic commerce, key parts of its plan to rely less on membership fees for revenue.
The Dulles, Va.-based company said it lost $154.8 million, or $1.64 a share, compared with a profit of $9.5 million, or 9 cents a share, in its fiscal 1996 second quarter.
America Online reported a 64 percent increase in quarterly revenues to $409.4 million from $249.1 million a year ago.

But the rise in revenues, driven by a record increase in the number of subscribers to nearly 8 million due to the switch to a flat rate, was offset by a previously announced $74.3 million charge for restructuring in October.
The company also announced a special charge of about $24 million for anticipated refunds and credits under an agreement reached Jan. 29 with state attorneys general from dozens of states.

The state proseuctors had met with America Online executives, and one state threatened to sue, after angry subscribers complained they got busy signals repeatedly when trying to dial in to the service.

The problem was the direct result of the switch to the flat rate of $19.95 a month for unlimited use of the service. Before, America Online charged $9.95 monthly for five hours, then charged for each additional hour -- a disincentive to spend more time online.
America Online said Thursday it had leased the 50,000 additional modems in addition to a $350 million programme to upgrade its network to address the problem.

The company, which has said it wants eventually to depend more on advertising and electronic commerce for revenues and less on subscriber fees, said those sources grew to $40 million in the latest quarter from about $24 million in the fiscal first quarter and just $13 million in the second quarter of fiscal 1996.
America Online announced its latest financial results after markets closed. Its stock dropped 37.5 cents to $38 on the New York Stock Exchange.
